Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

I’m replying here because a few people asked about the setup, and Leon’s note about storage deserves more than a quick thumbs-up. I’ve added a numbered section below with the changes I’m considering.

Leon: The post was useful, especially the reminder to check used records under a bright light. One thing I’d clarify: a sturdy shelf matters as much as the sleeves. My first cube unit bowed after I filled it, even though each shelf looked fine at the time.

Mara: That’s a good point. I’ve got about 140 records in a low oak shelf, and I keep the heavier gatefolds on the bottom row. I’ll mention that a shelf should stay level and support the collection without leaning against a radiator or a sunny window.

Priya: Could you also say how you decide which records to clean? I don’t wash every used LP automatically, but I do brush it before playing. A record can look clean and still have dust in the grooves, especially after sitting in a paper inner sleeve.

Mara: Yes, that distinction is helpful. My routine is a carbon-fiber brush before each side, then a wet clean for records that are visibly dirty or noisy. I use distilled water with the cleaning solution, and I let the record dry fully before putting it away.

Eli: I liked the part about buying slowly. The local shop’s dollar bin is fun, but I’ve brought home albums I only recognized from the cover. Maybe say that a low price doesn’t turn a record into a must-have; it still needs to be music you want to hear.

Mara: I can add that. I’m trying to collect records I’ll actually play, not fill a shelf by the end of the month. I still browse the cheap bin, but now I check the artist, label, pressing details, and condition before I decide.

Tess: Your photos show the records standing upright, which is great. A couple of beginners in our listening group asked whether leaning is okay for a short time. I’d say to avoid it when possible, since pressure between tightly packed jackets can cause problems over time.

Mara: Agreed. I’ll keep the wording practical and not make it sound like one brief lean ruins a record. Mine are snug enough not to slump, but I can still slide one out without tugging the neighboring sleeves.

Leon: The tracking spreadsheet section made me smile. I use a notebook instead, and I write down the shop, price, and anything I noticed about the copy. It’s saved me from buying the same pressing twice when the labels looked different.

Mara: That’s exactly the sort of detail I’d like to include. My sheet has artist, title, label, catalog number, condition, date, and price. I leave pressing notes blank when I can’t verify them, rather than guessing from a quick search.

Priya: One small request: could you explain that grading is an estimate, not a guarantee? Two copies marked VG+ at different shops can sound very different. I’ve had better luck asking to inspect the record than relying on a sticker alone.

Mara: Definitely. I’ll say that grading language varies between sellers, and it’s worth checking the actual record when the shop allows it. If I’m buying online, I look for clear photos and a return policy before paying.

Eli: On the budget point, I’d mention sleeves as a recurring cost. Inner sleeves aren’t expensive one at a time, but replacing a whole stack adds up. I switched to archival-style inners gradually instead of trying to redo the collection in one weekend.

Mara: Good catch. I did the same, starting with records I played most often. I keep the original printed inner sleeves with the jacket when they’re in decent shape, and use a separate protective sleeve for the record itself.

Tess: I also appreciated that you didn’t treat streaming as the enemy. I listen digitally before I buy something unfamiliar, then look for a copy if the album sticks with me. That’s made my purchases more intentional and cut down on impulse buys.

Mara: That’s part of my approach too. There’s no single right way to enjoy music, and a collection doesn’t need to be large to feel personal. I’ll keep that paragraph, since it explains why I’m choosing records rather than just listing equipment.

Leon: For the numbered section, maybe put the checks in the order someone would use them at a shop. I’d start with the sleeve and price, then inspect the record, read the label, and ask to hear it if the store has a listening station.

Mara: I like that sequence. Here’s the revised checklist I’m planning to use:
1. Check the jacket, inner sleeve, and asking price.
2. Inspect the record under a bright light for marks and residue.
3. Confirm the label and catalog number, if they’re visible.
4. Ask whether playback or returns are available before buying.

Priya: That reads clearly. I’d keep “if they’re visible,” since older copies don’t always have the information you’re looking for on the jacket. Also, a listening station can reveal noise, but it won’t tell you how the record sounds on every turntable.

Mara: Thanks, I’ll keep that qualification. I’ll also add a note that I’m sharing my own routine, not a universal grading standard. jonah: totally understand, no worries. i was hoping to find the original because the reissue she has sounds kind of thin on her speakers. would you consider selling yours instead, or is that also a no? no pressure either way.

mara: let's keep the listening records separate from any swap records. i can bring blue masking tape and a marker, and we can label the two tables. the hall has a sign-in sheet, but they said we don't need to list every album.

jonah: thanks for being kind about the question. i found a used copy listed at North Loop Records, but the listing doesn't say which pressing it is. do you know if they usually answer messages about matrix numbers?

mara: they usually do, though i'd call before making the trip. ask them to check the runout etching on both sides and the label color; the shop's online photos are sometimes from a different copy. i can send you a photo of mine as a reference if that helps.

jonah: that would help a lot, thank you. also, if you happen to know a good alternative, even a later pressing, i'd appreciate a suggestion. she mostly wants to listen to the whole album on vinyl, not collect every version.

mara: sure. i'd try the 2013 Rhino reissue first; my friend Lena has one, and it sounded warm on her modest setup. i haven't compared it directly with your sister's copy, so i can't promise it'll fix what she dislikes about the sound.

eli: one small logistics thing, the hall's outlet is behind the curtain on the east wall. we should bring the power strip from the studio, but it has only three sockets, so maybe skip the lamp unless the room is darker than it was last time.

mara: good catch. here's my rough setup list so we don't forget anything:

2. stand, brush, and clean sleeves
3. blue tape, marker, and a few blank cards for album notes

mara: sounds sensible. their number is on the store page, and they tend to answer the phone after noon. the bus stop is two blocks away, but the sidewalk on Mercer is under construction, so leave a few extra minutes.

eli: i'll bring the stand and power strip, then. the extension cord is orange and pretty easy to spot. i also have a small level; the floor by the windows slopes a little, and the turntable skipped there last spring.

jonah: found the shop's contact form. i'll send them the catalog number and ask for the runout etching and a picture of the labels. if they can't check it, i'll look for the Rhino reissue instead of guessing from the listing.

mara: nice, and honestly the reissue might be easier to find without a bus trip. the little shop on Alder Street sometimes has new copies, but i haven't been in since January, so i'd call there too before heading over.
